statement: A point mass $m$ moves with constant velocity $v$ along the straight line $y = d$ ($d > 0$) in the $xy$-plane. The magnitude of its angular momentum with respect to the origin $O$:

options.A: is zero because straight-line motion cannot have angular momentum
options.B: increases linearly as the particle moves farther from origin
options.C: is constant and equal to $m v d$ for all time
options.D: depends on the choice of $x$-coordinate and oscillates sinusoidally

solution_strategy: Apply definition of particle angular momentum L = r x p, use Cartesian coordinates to show L_z = x p_y - y p_x = -m v d, and observe that its magnitude |L| = m v d is time-invariant.
solution:
1. Position and Velocity Vectors:
The particle moves along the line $y = d$ parallel to the $x$-axis with constant velocity $\vec{v} = v\hat{i}$.
At any instant, its position vector with respect to origin $O$ is:
$$\vec{r}(t) = x(t)\hat{i} + d\hat{j}$$
Its linear momentum is:
$$\vec{p} = m\vec{v} = mv\hat{i}$$
2. Cross Product Evaluation:
The angular momentum about the origin is:
$$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p} = (x\hat{i} + d\hat{j}) \times (mv\hat{i}) = xmv(\hat{i} \times \hat{i}) + dmv(\hat{j} \times \hat{i}) = 0 - mvd\hat{k} = -mvd\hat{k}$$
3. Invariance in Time:
The magnitude of the angular momentum is:
$$|\vec{L}| = m v d$$
Because $m$, $v$, and the perpendicular distance $d$ are constants, $|\vec{L}|$ is strictly constant and independent of the $x$-coordinate for all time.
This directly confirms Option C and deconstructs misconception misc-rot-01.
assumptions: Inertial reference frame centered at origin O
Constant rectilinear velocity with zero net external force
intended_learning_objective: Directly dismantle the misconception that rectilinear uniform motion cannot possess angular momentum.

distractor_rationales.distractor_value: is zero because straight-line motion cannot have angular momentum
distractor_rationales.student_rationale: Student associates angular momentum exclusively with curved, circular, or rotational trajectories, believing rectilinear motion has L = 0.
distractor_rationales.physical_error: Angular momentum of a particle is defined by the cross product L = r x p relative to an origin. Even in rectilinear motion, as long as the line of motion does not pass through the origin (r_perp != 0), the cross product is non-zero (|L| = m v d != 0).

distractor_rationales.distractor_value: increases linearly as the particle moves farther from origin
distractor_rationales.student_rationale: Student reasons that because the radial distance r = sqrt(x^2 + d^2) grows as the particle moves away, the magnitude of angular momentum must grow proportionally.
distractor_rationales.physical_error: While radial distance r increases, the sine of the angle between r and v decreases proportionally: sin theta = d / r. Thus the perpendicular distance r_perp = r sin theta = d remains strictly constant: |L| = p r_perp = m v d.

distractor_rationales.distractor_value: depends on the choice of x-coordinate and oscillates sinusoidally
distractor_rationales.student_rationale: Student confuses angular position theta(t) = arctan(d / x(t)) with angular momentum, supposing that because angles change, L must oscillate.
distractor_rationales.physical_error: Torque about the origin is tau = r x F = 0 because velocity is constant (F = 0). By the angular momentum theorem dL/dt = tau = 0, L is strictly conserved in time and cannot oscillate.
